name: uber-tlc-foil-response
what_it_holds: FiveThirtyEight's classic FOIL-request dataset from NYC TLC: uber-raw-data-apr14.csv through sep14.csv (6 monthly files, ~4.5M Uber pickups Apr-Sep 2014, lat/lon/base), uber-raw-data-janjune-15.csv.zip (14.3M Uber pickups Jan-Jun 2015 with dispatching/affiliated base + location ID), Uber-Jan-Feb-FOIL.csv (aggregated daily Uber stats Jan-Feb 2015), and other-FHV-data/ covering 10 other NYC for-hire-vehicle companies plus other-FHV-data-jan-aug-2015.csv (daily pickups, 329 FHV companies, Jan-Aug 2015). NYC only, CC-BY-4.0 (parent fivethirtyeight/data repo), 735 stars, last updated Aug 2026 (repo itself, not the data vintage which is 2014-15).
why_useful: Point-in-time historical rideshare-volume snapshot for NYC predating most modern coverage; static and fully committed so it is trivially reproducible without a live pull, useful as an older baseline/backtest period for a ground-travel demand proxy (gap #10).
size_hint: ~19M Uber pickup rows + company-level FHV aggregates
themes: Rail and ground travel: Amtrak ridership, SNCF/DB/Trenitalia open data, Eurostar, bus (FlixBus), rideshare datasets (Uber Movement), NYC TLC airport trips, Chicago taxi
Awesome lists and curated catalogues: awesome-public-datasets, awesome-alternative-data, awesome-quant data, awesome-economics, awesome-tourism, awesome-real-estate, awesome-transportation-data
Gig-economy and platform-economy datasets (Uber/DoorDash/Etsy/Upwork public data) used as cross-platform consumer-behaviour reads
why_all: Point-in-time historical rideshare-volume snapshot for NYC predating most modern coverage; static and fully committed so it is trivially reproducible without a live pull, useful as an older baseline/backtest period for a ground-travel demand proxy (gap #10).

A city-level ground-transport activity proxy of the kind gap 10 asks for (airport/ground transport capacity and traffic); mainly useful as a worked example of NYC TLC/FHV data structure rather than current data (2014-15 vintage) - would need the live TLC portal for present quarters.

A real committed multi-company platform-trip dataset with a genuine method (FOIL request) for pulling non-Airbnb platform volumes; useful as a template for how a cross-platform gig-economy volume series could be constructed, and as a very old baseline for Uber's early growth curve. Data itself is a decade stale so it does not directly nowcast anything in gap list; value is methodological (FOIL-request approach to force disclosure of platform-level trip volumes) rather than current data.

name: deutsche-bahn-data
what_it_holds: Historical Deutsche Bahn train schedule, delay (minutes late), cancellation (arrival/departure separately), and station data. Raw API responses (parquet-wrapped XML/JSON) and monthly processed parquet files (20 columns: station, train ID, planned/actual times, delay, cancellation flag) for ~100 largest stations Jul 2024-Nov 2025, then all German stations Nov 2025-present (with a known 2025-11 to 2026-07 API-outage gap). Repo git history was rewritten to drop large files; full data now published on Hugging Face. CC BY 4.0 (DB) data licence.
why_useful: German/European rail punctuality and cancellation-rate time series at near-daily granularity — a EU ground-travel supply/demand and disruption proxy (gap #10) and a possible cancellation-rate methodology analogue for the RNPL/cancellation thesis (gap #3), even though the underlying business (rail) differs from STR bookings.
size_hint: Monthly parquet files, ~100-all stations x daily train movements
last_activity: active as of the 2026 README reference
themes: Rail and ground travel: Amtrak ridership, SNCF/DB/Trenitalia open data, Eurostar, bus (FlixBus), rideshare datasets (Uber Movement), NYC TLC airport trips, Chicago taxi

name: Joy-Pyne/Border_Crossing_Entry_Data
what_it_holds: 14-star notebook (Joy main.ipynb, 1.2MB) analysing the BTS/data.gov 'Border Crossing Entry Data' dataset (monthly US land-border crossings by port, state, measure -- pedestrians, personal vehicles, trucks, buses, trains -- for the US-Canada and US-Mexico borders, back to 1996, at data.bts.gov/Research-and-Statistics/Border-Crossing-Entry-Data/keg4-3bc2). Repo itself is a notebook, not a raw data mirror; the underlying dataset lives at the BTS/data.gov URL.
why_useful: Points directly to the official BTS Border Crossing Entry Data API/download (monthly, 1996-present, all US land ports, mode-level detail), which is a genuine and currently free national-level cross-border volume series relevant to gap #10; better to pull straight from data.bts.gov than via this notebook, but this and ~15 nearly-identical student repos (jiy15, GauravSingh7400, dipankar9794, TejPotu, etc. -- all re-analyzing the same data.gov dataset) confirm the source and its stable Socrata endpoint id (keg4-3bc2).
size_hint: source dataset is a multi-hundred-thousand-row Socrata table; this repo just has a notebook
geography: US land border ports (Canada and Mexico borders)
themes: Cross-border and visa data: Schengen visa statistics, ESTA, ETIAS, CBP wait times, passport index, border crossings BTS

name: py-gasbuddy
what_it_holds: Python library (18 stars, updated 7 Sep 2026, MIT) that queries GasBuddy's GraphQL API for station-level fuel prices by station ID, zip, or city; returns current regular/mid/premium/diesel price and station metadata. No historical data committed — a live pull method only.
why_useful: GasBuddy crowd-sourced gas prices are a leading, high-frequency (sub-daily) proxy for road-trip cost, which is the key substitute-cost driver for domestic drive-to leisure travel (gap #10, road/fuel theme); pairing weekly national averages with holiday-driving forecasts could feed a NA leisure-demand nowcast alongside TSA and nights data. Would need a scheduled pull to build a point-in-time series from today forward; no backfill.
themes: Road travel and fuel: gas prices (EIA, AAA), vehicle miles travelled, holiday driving, toll data
